questions.question: How does tin get into the food I eat?
questions.answer: In the modern food system tin is encountered overwhelmingly through tinplated steel cans, where the elemental tin lining dissolves into the food as inorganic tin in proportion to the food's acidity, the can's lacquering status, and storage time and temperature. Canned acidic foods such as fruit juices, fruit cocktails, tomato products, and pickled foods are the dominant dietary source of inorganic tin. A structurally separate organotin pathway comes mainly from seafood (legacy tributyltin antifouling paint), PVC food-contact materials and pipes, and historic organotin pesticide use ([[sources/atsdr2005-tin-toxicological-profile|ATSDR 2005]]).

questions.question: Is the tin in canned food dangerous to eat?
questions.answer: Inorganic tin, the form ingested from cans, is poorly absorbed (around 5 percent, with more than 90 percent excreted in feces) and causes toxicity mainly through local gastrointestinal irritation rather than systemic accumulation. In controlled human single-dose challenges, symptomatic effects appeared at roughly 1,000 to 1,400 ppm in fruit juices, which is well above the canned-product regulatory caps in any major jurisdiction ([[sources/benoy1971-tin-toxicity-canned-fruit-juices|Benoy 1971]]).

questions.question: Why does the wiki treat inorganic tin and organotins so differently?
questions.answer: The two classes differ in toxicity by approximately three orders of magnitude: the inorganic tin oral MRL is 0.3 mg/kg/day (intermediate) while the tributyltin oxide MRL is 0.0003 mg/kg/day (chronic). Organotins are lipophilic and well-absorbed, distribute systemically, and produce immune-system, central nervous system, and reproductive effects at exposures far below the inorganic tin symptomatic threshold ([[sources/atsdr2005-tin-toxicological-profile|ATSDR 2005]]). This species-distinction principle was established by [[sources/schafer1984-tin-toxic-heavy-metal-review|Schafer and Femfert 1984]], and total-tin measurement without speciation cannot be honestly mapped to toxicity-derived guidance.

questions.question: What are the legal limits for tin in canned food?
questions.answer: The EU sets binding inorganic-tin maximum levels under [[regulations/eu2023-contaminants-maximum-levels|EU 2023/915]]: 200 mg/kg in canned food other than beverages, 100 mg/kg in canned beverages, and 50 mg/kg in canned infant formula and baby food. Codex CXS 193-1995 sets looser limits of 250 mg/kg for general canned foods and 150 mg/kg for canned beverages. The U.S. has no equivalent FDA action level for tin in food and addresses it through Total Diet Study surveillance and contact-material guidance.

questions.question: Who is most at risk from dietary tin?
questions.answer: Infants and young children fed canned baby food are the principal vulnerable group for inorganic tin, which the EU recognizes with a 50 mg/kg cap set at one-quarter of the general canned-food limit. Frequent seafood consumers, particularly populations relying heavily on bivalves and crustaceans from coastal waters with legacy tributyltin contamination, are the principal group for organotins. Body-weight-normalized intake makes both groups more vulnerable than absolute concentrations alone suggest.

questions.question: How is tin measured in food, and can testing tell the two forms apart?
questions.answer: Atomic absorption spectrophotometry at 286.3 nm is the historical method for total tin, while ICP-MS after microwave digestion is the routine modern method; both produce total-tin values. Distinguishing inorganic tin from organotin requires speciation-preserving methods using gas chromatography or HPLC with element-specific detection, so a total-tin number alone does not identify which form is present.
